essence: How can the action, relation, universal, substance, direction, and time-cognitions be true (satya) rather than mere delusion, given that the external view (bāhyavāda) cannot account for them?

The passage establishes that the six cognitions (action, relation, universal, substance, direction, time) are true (satya) by stability and use, as one-many-support, because the reflexive awareness resting on the action-essence is stable and agrees with the intended action, unlike the double-moon case.

Abhinavagupta opens the dvitīyo vimarśaḥ with a maṅgala and a seven-verse plan: the Lord's un-thwarted freedom (apratihata svātantrya) in the form of action-power (kriyāśakti) is to be established, since the externally-refuted action-relation and related categories, which fail to fit in the external view, fit fully here.

The commentary explains: the action-cognition (kriyābuddhi) arising elsewhere than from consciousness-essence (saṃvittattva) is mere action-appearance (kriyābhāsa), cut off by māyā-power; but the action-essence (kriyātattva) as object is true (satya eva), because the reflexive awareness (vimarśa) resting on it is stable (sthira), not uprooted by the refuter (bādhaka), and agrees (saṃvādavān) with the intended action (grāmaprāpti).
